title: Surrogates and emulators: fast stand-ins
summary: A surrogate learns the input–output map of a slow simulator from a few runs, then answers new questions almost instantly. Where you sample and what you assume about smoothness decide its accuracy.
outcomes: explain what a surrogate model is and when it pays off
build a simple surrogate by interpolating a few runs
describe how the number and placement of runs affect accuracy
give transport examples of expensive models worth emulating
narration_en: Many scientific models are slow. A detailed traffic simulation of a city, a climate and energy model such as GCAM, or a crash simulation can take hours for a single run. Yet we often want thousands of runs: to optimise a design, explore policies, or quantify uncertainty. A surrogate model, also called an emulator or metamodel, solves this. We run the expensive model at a few carefully chosen inputs, then fit a fast model to these input–output pairs. The surrogate answers new questions in milliseconds. Common surrogates include radial basis functions, Gaussian processes, polynomial chaos and neural networks. Accuracy depends on how many runs we make, where we place them, and how smooth the true relationship is. Placing runs evenly, or using space-filling designs such as Latin hypercubes, usually beats random placement. A good surrogate also says where it is unsure, so we know where to run the full model next. In this module you will emulate an expensive function with a handful of runs and see how placement and smoothness matter.
narration_ar: كثير من النماذج العلمية بطيئة. فمحاكاة مرورية مفصلة لمدينة، أو نموذج للمناخ والطاقة مثل GCAM، أو محاكاة اصطدام، قد تستغرق ساعات للتشغيل الواحد. ومع ذلك نحتاج غالباً إلى آلاف التشغيلات: لتحسين تصميم، أو استكشاف سياسات، أو تقدير عدم اليقين. والنموذج البديل، ويسمى أيضاً المحاكي أو النموذج الفوقي، يحل هذه المشكلة. نشغّل النموذج المكلف عند مدخلات قليلة مختارة بعناية، ثم نبني نموذجاً سريعاً على أزواج المدخلات والمخرجات هذه، فيجيب البديل عن أسئلة جديدة في أجزاء من الثانية. ومن البدائل الشائعة دوال الأساس الشعاعية، والعمليات الغاوسية، وفوضى كثيرات الحدود، والشبكات العصبية. وتتوقف الدقة على عدد التشغيلات، ومواضعها، ومدى نعومة العلاقة الحقيقية. ووضع التشغيلات بانتظام، أو استخدام تصاميم تملأ الفضاء مثل المكعب اللاتيني الفائق، يتفوق عادة على الوضع العشوائي. والبديل الجيد يخبرنا أيضاً أين يكون غير متأكد، فنعرف أين نشغّل النموذج الكامل بعد ذلك. ستحاكي في هذه الوحدة دالة مكلفة بعدد قليل من التشغيلات.

tour.text: Start with a model that is accurate but slow.
Run it at a few chosen inputs.
Fit a fast surrogate to the results.
Use the surrogate for thousands of queries.
Its uncertainty tells you where to run the full model next.

sections.heading: When surrogates pay off
sections.html: If one run takes an hour and a study needs 10,000 runs, the full model needs more than a year of computing. A surrogate built from 20 runs answers the rest in seconds. Surrogates pay off when runs are expensive, inputs are few (roughly up to 20), and the response is reasonably smooth.

sections.heading: Interpolating with radial basis functions
sections.html: A radial basis function (RBF) surrogate adds a bump centred at each run: ŝ(x) = Σ wⱼ exp(−(ε(x − xⱼ))²). The weights are chosen so that ŝ passes exactly through every run. ε sets how wide the bumps are: too narrow and the surrogate dips between runs; too wide and the system becomes ill-conditioned. In the explorer, 6 evenly spaced runs give an error of about 0.05, and 10 runs about 0.006.

sections.heading: Designing the runs
sections.html: Where you run matters as much as how many. Evenly spaced or Latin hypercube designs cover the input space; random designs leave gaps. Adaptive (active-learning) designs run the full model where the surrogate is most uncertain, which is where Gaussian processes (module 2.6) help. In Go 3 you will emulate a GCAM transport output this way.

explorer.intro: An 'expensive' model takes one minute per run. Build a surrogate from a few runs.
explorer.predict: How many evenly spaced runs do you need for an error below 0.05?

code.title: A radial basis function surrogate
code.source:
import numpy as np
f = lambda x: np.sin(3*x) + 0.3*x**2          # stand-in for an expensive model
xt = np.linspace(0, 3, 151)
for n in [4, 6, 10]:
    xr = np.linspace(0, 3, n); eps = 1.5
    K = np.exp(-(eps*(xr[:, None] - xr))**2) + 1e-8*np.eye(n)
    w = np.linalg.solve(K, f(xr))
    s = np.exp(-(eps*(xt[:, None] - xr))**2) @ w
    print(f'{n:2d} runs: surrogate error {np.sqrt(np.mean((s - f(xt))**2)):.4f}')
code.explain: More runs, smaller error, for a smooth function.
code.expected:
4 runs: surrogate error 0.5820
 6 runs: surrogate error 0.0522
10 runs: surrogate error 0.0060

takeaways: A surrogate is a fast model trained on a few runs of a slow one.
It pays off when runs are expensive and many queries are needed.
Accuracy depends on the number and placement of runs and on smoothness.
Uncertainty-aware surrogates tell you where to run the full model next.

glossary.def: A fast approximate model trained on input–output pairs of a slower model; also emulator or metamodel.
A function that depends only on distance from a centre, used as a building block for interpolation.
The choice of inputs at which to run a model or experiment.
A space-filling design that spreads runs across each input's range.
Choosing new runs where the current model is most uncertain.
